One kit, from layout to interaction

Start with components, page blocks and dashboard examples that share a design language. Underneath, two independent layers let you use the whole kit or bring just the styling or behaviour into an existing project.

Colibri Kit the family
Colibri CSS= the look

Colours, fonts, spacing, layout, dark mode. A stylesheet you link once.

+
Colibri UI= the behaviour

Dialogs that open, menus that drop down, tabs that switch, with keyboard and screen-reader support.

What does "headless" mean? A headless component does the work (opening, closing, focus, keyboard, accessibility) but ships with no visual design. You decide how it looks. Think of a car's engine and steering without the body: it drives, and you choose the paint. In Colibri Kit, Colibri UI is headless, and Colibri CSS is the paint. "Headless" describes the UI components, never the stylesheet.

Colibri CSS

@colibri-kit/css

The stylesheet. This is the look, and it is not headless. A token-first stylesheet: modern reset, OKLCH colour tokens from one hue, fluid type, built-in dark mode, seven layout primitives and a few opt-in components, all in cascade layers.

  • Cascade layers: your CSS always wins
  • Container queries, :has(), native nesting
  • light-dark() dark mode, clamp() fluid scale
  • Primitives, not utilities: .stack .grid .split .cluster
Colibri CSS library page →

Colibri UI

@colibri-kit/ui

Headless components: they handle behaviour and accessibility but come with no built-in look, so they never fight your design. Wire them with attributes: data-ui="dialog", data-ui-part="trigger". Use them through JS, custom elements or FreeMarker macros, styled by your tokens.

  • Dialogs, menus, tabs, comboboxes, date pickers, toasts…
  • AI elements: chat, prompt input, reasoning trace
  • Sidebar, login and signup blocks
  • Keyboard & screen-reader support built in
Browse every component →

One page, two layers of the same idea

Write the HTML you'd write anyway. Add data-ui where you need behaviour. Set a few tokens where you want your brand. That's the whole workflow.

The bridge stylesheet maps Colibri UI's --ui-* tokens to Colibri CSS's --c-* tokens, so components, layout and content share one palette, one radius scale and one dark mode.

<!-- a styled, accessible dialog, no framework -->
<div data-ui="dialog">
  <button class="btn" data-ui-part="trigger">Invite</button>
  <dialog data-ui-part="content" class="card stack">
    <h2 data-ui-part="title">Invite a teammate</h2>
    <div class="field"><label for="e">Email</label>
      <input id="e" type="email" required></div>
    <div class="cluster"><button class="btn">Send</button>
      <button class="btn" data-variant="ghost" data-ui-part="close">Cancel</button></div>
  </dialog>
</div>
[#import "/ui/ui.ftl" as ui]
[@ui.dialog trigger="Invite" title="Invite a teammate"]
  <div class="field"><label for="e">Email</label>
    <input id="e" type="email" required></div>
  <div class="cluster">[@ui.close]Send[/@ui.close]
    [@ui.close variant="ghost"]Cancel[/@ui.close]</div>
[/@ui.dialog]
import { Dialog, Part } from "@colibri-kit/ui/react";

<Dialog>
  <Part name="trigger" as="button" className="btn">Invite</Part>
  <Part name="content" as="dialog" className="card stack">
    <Part name="title" as="h2">Invite a teammate</Part>
    <div className="field"><label htmlFor="e">Email</label>
      <input id="e" type="email" required /></div>
    <div className="cluster"><button className="btn">Send</button>
      <Part name="close" as="button" className="btn" data-variant="ghost">Cancel</Part></div>
  </Part>
</Dialog>

Why choose Colibri Kit?

Keep the design in CSS, the structure in HTML, and your choice of framework open.

Coming from shadcn/ui?

shadcn/ui uses Tailwind. Colibri uses semantic CSS and framework-independent behaviour. Choose Colibri for server templates, mixed stacks or a Tailwind-free workflow. Already committed to React and Tailwind? shadcn/ui may be the closer fit.

Readable markup, reusable design

Describe components with semantic classes and attributes. Keep colours, spacing and variants in CSS and tokens, so a design change does not mean editing utility strings across your templates.

Start without a build pipeline

Link the stylesheet and import the behaviour modules in a plain HTML page. No Tailwind compiler or frontend framework is required. Add Colibri to your existing application without rebuilding it around a new stack.

Platform-native

Layers, :has(), container queries, nesting, light-dark(), OKLCH and native <dialog>: the browser does the heavy lifting.

Re-colour in one line

:root { --c-hue: 160 } changes the base palette. Add data-colibri-theme to a section to derive its palette from a local hue. For a whole new look (shapes, tabs, density), use a theme pack.

Works with server templates

Plain HTML, FreeMarker macros and custom elements. No SPA required, no hydration.

Accessibility foundations

Behavior controllers provide keyboard controls and ARIA wiring; CSS supplies focus rings and reduced-motion tokens. Test your content, contrast and integrations before release.

Theme packs

A theme pack is a complete look: corner shapes, typography, tab and accordion style, density, shadows and motion, plus colours. Colour (the hue slider and accent) is separate and layers on top of any pack. Pick a pack in the header, or open the kitchen sink with ?theme=.

Glacier

Crisp and dense. Tight 4px corners, underline tabs, skinny hairline accordions, flat cards, fast motion. Slate + teal.

Kitchen sink →

Ember

Soft and roomy. Pill buttons and pill tabs, fat card-style accordions, deep warm shadows, springy motion. Terracotta + amber.

Kitchen sink →

Midnight

Sharp and technical. 2px corners, boxed uppercase tab segments, bordered accordions with a glowing accent rail, monospace headings. Ink + violet.

The token cheatsheet

Colour

--c-hue --c-brand --c-accent --c-bg --c-surface --c-sunken --c-fg --c-muted --c-line --c-ok --c-warn --c-bad

Type

--c-text-xs … --c-text-3xl (fluid), --c-font, --c-font-mono, --c-leading

Space

--c-space-3xs … --c-space-2xl (fluid)

Shape & depth

--c-radius-s --c-radius --c-radius-l --c-shadow-s --c-shadow --c-shadow-l

Motion

--c-dur-fast --c-dur --c-dur-slow --c-ease --c-ease-out --c-ease-spring, all 0 with reduced motion

Primitives

.stack .cluster .grid .split .switcher .center .reel .prose, tuned with --gap --min --side --at

Use it your way

Same components, three ways to write them. Pick a tab once; every example on the page follows.

1. Add it to your project

<!-- 1. the look -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://colibri.l3v.ai/css/colibri.css">
<!-- 2. component styling + shared tokens -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://colibri.l3v.ai/ui/themes/colibri.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://colibri.l3v.ai/css/colibri-ui-bridge.css">
<!-- 3. behaviour: every data-ui element wires itself -->
<script type="module" src="https://colibri.l3v.ai/ui/src/core/auto.js"></script>
[#-- layout.ftl --]
[#import "/colibri/ui.ftl" as ui]
<link rel="stylesheet" href="${base}/css/colibri.css">
<script type="module" src="${base}/ui/src/core/auto.js"></script>

[#-- then use macros anywhere --]
[@ui.button variant="outline"]Save[/@ui.button]
// Install from source (npm registry releases are not published yet):
// git clone https://github.com/levancho/colibri-kit.git vendor/colibri-kit
// npm install ./vendor/colibri-kit ./vendor/colibri-kit/packages/colibri-css
import "@colibri-kit/ui/themes/colibri.css";
import "@colibri-kit/css";
import "@colibri-kit/css/bridge";
import { Dialog, Tabs, Part, cx } from "@colibri-kit/ui/react";
// No auto-init in React: each wrapper wires itself on mount.

3. Tabs

Live
Colibri CSS: colours, type, spacing, layout.
Colibri UI: keyboard, focus, open and close.
<div data-ui="tabs" data-default-value="look">
  <div data-ui-part="list" aria-label="Kit parts">
    <button data-ui-part="trigger" data-value="look">Look</button>
    <button data-ui-part="trigger" data-value="behaviour">Behaviour</button>
  </div>
  <div data-ui-part="panel" data-value="look">Colibri CSS</div>
  <div data-ui-part="panel" data-value="behaviour">Colibri UI</div>
</div>
[@ui.tabs default="look" tabs=[
    {"value":"look", "label":"Look"},
    {"value":"behaviour", "label":"Behaviour"}]]
  [@ui.panel value="look"]Colibri CSS[/@ui.panel]
  [@ui.panel value="behaviour"]Colibri UI[/@ui.panel]
[/@ui.tabs]
const [tab, setTab] = useState("look");

<Tabs defaultValue="look" onChange={(e) => setTab(e.detail.value)}>
  <Part name="list" aria-label="Kit parts">
    <Part name="trigger" as="button" value="look">Look</Part>
    <Part name="trigger" as="button" value="behaviour">Behaviour</Part>
  </Part>
  <Part name="panel" value="look">Colibri CSS</Part>
  <Part name="panel" value="behaviour">Colibri UI</Part>
</Tabs>

One way to style: your CSS, our tokens.

Colibri CSS is not a Tailwind alternative. We want you off long chains of utility classes, not on a new set of them. You write normal HTML (or JSX) with a few meaningful class names, set variants with attributes, and keep the design in CSS. HTML, FreeMarker and React all use the exact same markup.

1 · Primitives

A few layout words

.stack, .cluster, .grid, .split, .center… plus components like .card, .btn, .badge. About a dozen names you can learn in five minutes.

2 · Attributes

Variants and spacing as attributes

data-variant="ghost", data-tone="ok", data-gap="l". Every value is a design token, so there are no magic numbers and a re-brand still changes everything.

3 · Your CSS

Anything else goes in CSS

Write a normal rule with var(--c-*) tokens. Colibri sits in cascade layers, so your CSS always wins without !important.

<section class="stack" data-gap="m">
  <h2>Team</h2>
  <div class="grid" style="--min: 14rem">
    <article class="card team-card">…</article>
  </div>
  <div class="cluster" data-justify="end">
    <button class="btn" data-variant="ghost">Cancel</button>
    <button class="btn">Invite</button>
  </div>
</section>

/* your CSS: one meaningful rule, not ten classes */
.team-card { border-inline-start: 3px solid var(--c-accent); }
<section class="stack" data-gap="m">
  <h2>Team</h2>
  <div class="grid" style="--min: 14rem">
    [#list team as p]<article class="card team-card">${p.name}</article>[/#list]
  </div>
  <div class="cluster" data-justify="end">
    [@ui.button variant="ghost"]Cancel[/@ui.button]
    [@ui.button]Invite[/@ui.button]
  </div>
</section>
// same primitives, same attributes: just className instead of class
<section className="stack" data-gap="m">
  <h2>Team</h2>
  <div className="grid" style={{ "--min": "14rem" }}>
    {team.map((p) => <article key={p.id} className="card team-card">{p.name}</article>)}
  </div>
  <div className="cluster" data-justify="end">
    <button className="btn" data-variant="ghost">Cancel</button>
    <button className="btn">Invite</button>
  </div>
</section>
Why not utility classes? With class="flex flex-col gap-4 p-6 rounded-xl shadow" the design ends up scattered through every template, and you need a compiler to keep it small. Colibri keeps markup readable (class="card stack"), keeps the design in one stylesheet, and needs no build step. One small helper file, .muted, .truncate and .visually-hidden, is the only "utility" set, and it stays tiny on purpose.
